en_segments: (Siman 173, seif 2) If he had produce such that, were he to sell it in the market and receive payment immediately, he would sell it for 10, but if the buyer sought to purchase it and pay immediately he would buy it for 12, it is permitted to sell it to him on credit for 12, since its present value is 12. All of this is the language of the Rambam in chapter 8 of Hilchos Malveh, halacha 4. In my humble opinion, it is explicit from the Rambam there and from the Tur that even if it is presently worth 12, it is forbidden to state explicitly, "If you pay now, it is yours for less, but if you pay later, for 12." Nevertheless, there is concern that one may say this even when it is not presently worth 12. This entire seif is the language of the Rambam, and there it is explicit that he discusses an unspecified sale, for immediately above, in halacha 2, he writes: "If he sold him merchandise for 12, its actual value, on condition that he pay after a period of time, he may say to him, 'Pay me immediately and I will take from you only 10.'" End of his words. Thus, even when 12 is its actual value, he permits saying explicitly, "If you pay now, for less," only after the sale was first made without such a stipulation, because it is then like the seller is buying it back from him. We therefore learn that according to the Rambam, this is permitted only where the deferred price is the present value and the initial sale was unspecified. If he states the two prices explicitly, the fact that it is worth the higher amount does not help. Likewise, where it is not worth that amount, an unspecified sale does not help according to the Rambam, as the Maggid Mishneh and the Beit Yosef explain his view. On this latter point the Tur and Shulchan Aruch disagree with him, and hold that where an item has no fixed market price and its valuation is not known, it is permitted in an unspecified sale to sell it at a higher price for payment at a specified later date, as written at the beginning of this siman. Therefore, in the following seif, when they cite the Rambam's law, "If he sold him merchandise for 12," etc., the Tur and Shulchan Aruch omit the word "at its value," because according to them even if it is not presently worth that much, an unspecified sale is permitted. But on the present point they do not disagree with the Rambam. What is written in this seif, that if he had produce, etc., "it is permitted to sell it to him on credit for 12," means specifically in an unspecified sale. This is the same as what was written in seif 1, that he may sell it at a higher price for payment at a specified later date. It is forbidden, however, to say, "Pay me immediately for less," unless he already sold it to him without stipulation, as written in the following seif. This is also explicit in the Tur in this siman, where he writes: "With rental it is permitted even if he states it explicitly, for example, if he rents him something worth 12 for 10 and says to him, 'If you pay now,' etc., it is permitted." See there. This explicitly proves that regarding a sale it is forbidden to state, "If you pay now," etc., even where the item is actually worth the higher amount. Otherwise, what distinction would there be between a sale and a rental? Know that the Tzemach Tzedek permits this, as the Taz wrote in Orach Chayyim, siman 247, in the name of one rabbi, through a sale of objects. This also appears to be the view of the Peri Megadim there. He explains that whenever the transaction is not structured as an actual loan and has the form of a sale, the Torah was not particular about it and it is permitted. This also appears from Beis Lechem Yehudah at the end of Hilchos Ribbis. The Bechor Shor likewise rules this way and disputes the Taz in Orach Chayyim, and this is also the view of the Noda B'Yehuda, as I will write shortly. In Atzei Chaim on Choshen Mishpat, siman 72, he cites Knesset HaGedolah that if an item came into the lender's possession by way of a sale in order to avoid ribbis, and he promised the borrower that whenever the borrower brought the money he would sell the item back to him, then if the collateral was lost the borrower has no claim against the lender. This also appears from the Bechor Shor, who holds that for this reason the arrangement is permitted with movable property, because it is a complete sale. If the item is lost, the lender does not pay the seller the excess value, and only if the item still exists does he return it to him. Thus, even with respect to the seller it is considered a sale. The Noda B'Yehuda, Mahadura Tinyana, Yoreh De'ah, siman 75, writes similarly. There is also proof from the Rambam, who writes in chapter 11 of Hilchos Mechirah, halacha 10, regarding movable property that the sale remains valid and he returns the item when they stipulated a particular time or when the original seller gives him the money. The Lechem Mishneh there struggled to explain what distinction there is between land and movable property. According to what the Bechor Shor and the Noda B'Yehuda wrote, however, the matter is well understood.

(Siman 210, seif 3) One who makes a vow and retracts it, etc., within toch k'dei dibbur of his vow. See Shach, seif katan 7: within toch k'dei dibbur of his vow, but not within toch k'dei dibbur of their protest. See the responsum of the Rashba cited in Choshen Mishpat, siman 80, that toch k'dei dibbur of another person's speech is not considered part of one's own speech.
